Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:195: The sixth part — one who has it in his power to protest and does not protest, and has no rebuke in his mouth, and does not fix his eye upon or take heed of the deeds of sinners, and does not become for them a man who rebukes. Now, we have been commanded to root out evil from the midst of our people, as it is said (Deuteronomy 13:6), "So shall you root out the evil from your midst." And our Sages said: whoever has it in his power to protest against the members of his household and does not protest is held accountable for the members of his household; whoever has it in his power to protest against the people of his city and does not protest is held accountable for the people of his city; whoever has it in his power to protest against the whole world and does not protest is held accountable for the whole world. And it is said (Leviticus 26:37), "and they shall stumble, one man over his brother" — our Sages expounded this (Sanhedrin 27b): each man, because of his brother's iniquity. And they said (Shevuot 39a): all of Israel are sureties one for another.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:196: The seventh part — one who sees that the people of his place are stiff-necked, and says in his heart, Perhaps they will not listen if I speak straight words to them and fill my mouth with rebukes — and therefore withholds his mouth. Behold, he shall bear his iniquity, for he never even attempted to rebuke and to warn. Yet perhaps, had their spirit been stirred, they would have awakened from the sleep of their folly, and their error would not have lodged with them. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 55a), concerning what is written (Ezekiel 9:4), "and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry, etc." — the attribute of Justice said: Even though these men are utterly righteous and fulfilled the Torah, they should have protested and did not protest. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is revealed and known before Me that even had they protested, [the sinners] would not have accepted it from them. The attribute of Justice said: Master of the universe, if it is revealed before You, they themselves did not know whether the people would listen to their voice or refuse. And the Blessed Name then commanded (Ezekiel 9:6), "and begin at My sanctuary" — meaning the righteous, the sanctified ones, for they were punished for not having protested. And it is said (Leviticus 19:17), "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." And if the matter is manifest to all, known, tested, and examined, that the sinner hates discipline and will not listen to the voice of those who instruct him, nor incline his ear to his teachers — of this it is said (Proverbs 9:8), "Rebuke not a scoffer, lest he hate you." And they said (Yevamot 65b): just as it is a mitzvah to say a thing that will be heeded, so it is a mitzvah not to say a thing that will not be heeded. And they said (Beitzah 30a): it is better that they sin inadvertently than deliberately.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:197: The eighth part — a man who hears people speaking evil speech, or hears any mouth speaking vileness, or sits in the company of mockers who scorn Torah and mitzvot, and knows that they are stubborn and thorny, and that if he rebukes them they will not heed his words — therefore he puts his hand over his mouth. This too is punished, for he should not answer fools according to their folly, lest they say of him that he is like them and that he has agreed with their words; how much more is he obligated to answer and rebuke them, to give due weight to the Torah and the commandments they have scorned and mocked, and to be zealous for the honor of the innocent and righteous of whom they speak.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:198: And this is one of the things for the sake of which a man is obligated to abandon the company of the wicked — for he will be punished by continually hearing their evil words and growing weary of answering them. And this matter is explicit in the words of Solomon, as it is said (Proverbs 24:1), "Envy not evil men, nor desire to be with them; for their heart devises destruction, and their lips speak of mischief." Its meaning: you shall bear iniquity through their sin, for you will continually hear their evil words and remain as one who is silent.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:199: The ninth part — one who honors the wicked out of a way of peace. Indeed, he does not speak well of the wicked man, nor does he conduct himself with such honor toward him that people would think he honors him because he is precious and honored in his eyes; for he grants him no honor except in the manner that people honor the rich — out of flattery and in hope of benefit, because their way has prospered, not because of their own inherent worth. And even so, there is sin and guilt in this matter, for even though it is permitted to honor the rich, it is not so for the wicked, as it is said (Job 40:11-12), "and look on every one who is proud, and abase him... look on every one who is proud, humble him, and tread down the wicked in their place." But this part is permitted out of worry lest the wicked man cause harm and bring about loss, at a time when the hand of the wicked is powerful and his hour is insolent, and it is not in our power to subdue him or drive him off with our own strength. Therefore it is permitted to honor him in the manner that people honor men of a raised arm, out of dread and fear — by rising and showing respect and the like — but he should not praise him or speak well of him to other people. And so our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 41b): it is permitted to flatter the wicked in this world.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:200: And this is the matter of the faction of those who speak evil speech. Our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Arachin 15b): whoever speaks evil speech is as though he denied the fundamental principle [of faith], as it is said (Psalms 12:5), "who have said, With our tongue we shall prevail; our lips are with us; who is lord over us?" Therefore they regarded him as though he had denied the fundamental principle, for he brings about and causes great harm and much evil to his fellows, making their reputation stink in the eyes of the people, or through other ways of loss. It is not conceivable that a man would prepare for his fellow an instrument of destruction and harm more bitter than death, without gaining for himself any benefit or monetary profit thereby, unless his inclination has ensnared his soul and he has cast off the yoke of Heaven from himself and severed its bonds — as it is said in the psalm concerning the coming of the Ziphites when they said to Saul, etc.: "O God, presumptuous men have risen against me, and a company of violent men have sought my soul, and have not set You before them." And our Sages of blessed memory explained "and have not set You before them": for they intended that Saul bless them, as he said to them (I Samuel 23:21), "Blessed are you of the Lord, for you have had compassion on me" — and they did not set God before them, He who wrote in His Torah (Deuteronomy 27:24), "Cursed be he who strikes his fellow in secret." And it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:11), "and there is no advantage to the master of the tongue," and it is said concerning Doeg (Psalms 52:4-5), "Your tongue devises mischief, etc.; you love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking righteousness, selah." And they explained in the Midrash on Psalms: What benefit and what profit did you gain from speaking evil speech? For surely you did not need money, since you were already wealthy, as it is said of him (I Samuel 21:8), "the chief of Saul's herdsmen." It is nothing but that you loved evil more than good, and falsehood more than speaking righteousness, for you cast off its yoke. And it is said (Proverbs 6:30), "Men do not despise a thief if he steals, etc.", and it is said afterward, "He who commits adultery lacks a heart, etc." — meaning that he [the master of the tongue] is worse than the thief, who must satisfy his soul when he is hungry. And our Sages of blessed memory said that the master of evil speech is worse than both, since he sins a great sin without any benefit at all, as it is said (Psalms 120:3), "What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, O deceitful tongue?"
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:201: And the second reason the one who speaks evil speech is considered as though he had denied the fundamental principle: because he says in his heart that his lips are in his own power, and since there is no deed involved, he is master over his own tongue; and he resolves in his own mind that he need not restrain the breath of his lips from whatever rises in his spirit, and that only his other limbs are not in his own power to sin with — in the sense of what is said (Psalms 12:5), "our lips are with us; who is lord over us?" He should not say this, but rather, Where is God my Maker, all of whose creature's movements are given over to Him — not one of them is missing, all are subjugated to do His will; only speech and the expression of the lips are in our own power! Not so the wicked who sin in other transgressions, for they know that it is evil and bitter to forsake the Name, but they are drawn after their desire and their overpowering inclination, and this distresses them. And our Sages said that evil speech is weighed as equal to three transgressions, namely idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed. Concerning idolatry it is said (Exodus 32:31), "Alas, this people have sinned a great sin"; concerning sexual immorality it is said (Genesis 39:9), "how then can I do this great wickedness"; concerning bloodshed it is said (Genesis 4:13), "My iniquity is too great to bear." Yet concerning evil speech it is said (Psalms 12:4), "May the Lord cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:202: Now we must explain to you how it is possible that the iniquity of evil speech should exceed these three. Is it not that our Sages of blessed memory said, concerning each of these three, that one should be killed rather than transgress them? And they said that idolatry is so grave that whoever acknowledges it is as though he denied the whole Torah, and that the apostate to idolatry is an apostate to the whole Torah entirely. And when you set your heart to their words of blessed memory, you will find for it several roots and several aspects.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:203: The first — that the master of the tongue repeats his folly: ten times a day he humiliates, defames, and shames, speaking excessive words and striking in secret — and who can set a limit to his punishment, for the master of the tongue sets no bound to his words? Since even a light transgression becomes very heavy when the folly is repeated many times, as we have already stated — how much more so a great sin and a grievous evil. And as they said, of blessed memory, that evil speech is weighed as equal to three transgressions — its meaning is: equal to one who transgresses those three at the moment his inclination overpowers him, not equal to the apostate who has removed himself from the community to transgress them continually at all times.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:204: And the second — the master of the tongue finds teshuvah difficult, since he has taught his tongue to speak lies and has sent forth his mouth in evil; through the abundance of habit he is no longer master over his own spirit, and it is as though his tongue itself brings about the thought, in the sense of what is said (Psalms 52:4), "Your tongue devises mischief," and it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:12), "but the lips of a fool consume him," and it is said (Proverbs 18:7), "the mouth of a fool is his ruin (mechitah)." "Mechitah" is in the sense of fear and dread — meaning that the fool should fear and dread the fury of his own tongue, lest he be ensnared by it, just as he would fear his enemy, since his lips are not in his own power.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:205: And the third — the master of the tongue regards his own sin as light, for he says it is merely a matter of the lips, and does not turn his attention to its many harms; therefore he does not turn back from his evil way. And even if he does turn back, his teshuvah is not complete, for he does not recognize the greatness of his sin — for complete teshuvah, to be cleansed of a great transgression, requires that the burning of grief blaze within his soul like the blaze of fire.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:206: And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 21:24), "Proud, haughty, scoffer is his name, who deals in the fury of pride." Its meaning: the scoffer whose presumption has overpowered him to strike with his tongue, out of his pride and arrogance, his fury and his wrath — do not say he strikes only with his tongue and not in deed, for know surely that he acts in the fury of presumption. Its meaning: if he cannot strike his enemies with his tongue, but can strike them in deed, he will strike through transgression without pity — as our Sages of blessed memory said concerning the matter of Doeg: when Saul commanded that the priests be struck, and his men refused to strike them, he said to Doeg, You struck with the tongue; you shall strike with the sword — as it is said (I Samuel 22:18), "Turn and fall upon the priests."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:207: And the fourth — if the master of the tongue returns in teshuvah, he must seek forgiveness from those upon whom the fury of his tongue was poured, yet he does not remember the number of them all, for he has caused pain to many, and grieved many souls. And many of those he does remember he has troubled, and they do not know that he brought evil upon them; he is ashamed to make it known to them and open their ears to the harm he did them, for he strikes and his blow is unknown — in the sense of what is said (Psalms 120:3-4), "What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, O deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty." Therefore evil speech is compared to an arrow, for one who draws a bow many times sends his arrows at a man, yet it is not known who struck him.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:208: And it is further compared to an arrow for another reason: for one who draws a sword, if his compassion is aroused for the man when he pleads with him, can return his sword to its sheath — not so one who shoots an arrow, for it is no longer in his power to bring it back. So it is with the master of evil speech: once the word has left his mouth, he cannot repair it. And sometimes he speaks of a blemish in a family, and thereby damages all the generations that come after — and no forgiveness can reach him for this. Therefore our Sages of blessed memory said that one who speaks of a blemish in a family has no atonement forever. And behold, one who sends forth his tongue speaks even against the holy ones who are on earth, for over whom has his evil not passed continually? And our Sages of blessed memory already said that the heretic has no share in the World to Come.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:209: And the fifth — evil speech brings its master to give his mouth over to speak error even against the Name, as it is said (Psalms 73:9), "They have set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walks through the earth." And there is no transgression whose punishment matches the punishment of one who speaks such things. And our Sages said: our forefathers tested [the Lord] with ten trials, and in none of them was their sentence sealed except for evil speech, as it is said (Numbers 14:28), "As surely as I live, says the Lord, as you have spoken in My ears, so will I do to you, etc.", and it is said (Deuteronomy 1:34), "And the Lord heard the voice of your words, and was angry, and swore, saying, etc.", and it is said (Malachi 2:17), "You have wearied the Lord with your words." And David the king, peace upon him, said (Psalms 50:16-20), "But to the wicked man God says, What have you to do with declaring My statutes, that you have taken My covenant in your mouth? ... if you saw a thief, you ran with him, etc.... You give your mouth to evil, and your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother." Behold, you have learned from this that the Torah is not a defense for masters of evil speech, nor for the apostate who steals and commits adultery, and that they are not fit to occupy themselves with Torah. And our Sages of blessed memory said: since Doeg spoke evil speech, even his wisdom did not stand by him, nor did his Torah protect him. And what our Sages of blessed memory said, that a transgression extinguishes a mitzvah but no transgression extinguishes Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 6:23), "For the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light" — this was said concerning one who commits a transgression by way of chance, not concerning one who casts off the yoke of the warning against the transgression from himself.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:210: And consider how great is the iniquity of people who speak evil speech. It is not enough that their great iniquity is that they withhold their lips and restrain their tongue from speaking words of Torah — for they further corrupt themselves by speaking evil speech. And David the king, peace upon him, said (Psalms 119:23), "Princes also sat and spoke against me; your servant meditated on your statutes." Its meaning: they are idle from meditating on Your statutes, and speak evil speech and speak against me, while I meditate on Your statutes. And our Sages said the remedy for evil speech, to be saved from it, is that a man occupy himself with Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 15:4), "A healing tongue is a tree of life." And this is what is said (Psalms 39:2), "I will guard my ways, that I sin not with my tongue; I will keep my mouth with a bridle, etc." — our Sages of blessed memory explained that the bridle is occupation with Torah. And our Sages said: the Assembly of Israel is both beloved and hated for its voice — beloved for its voice, as it is said (Song of Songs 2:14), "Let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet"; and hated for its voice, as it is said (Jeremiah 12:8), "she has uttered her voice against Me, therefore I have hated her." And this is what is said (Proverbs 18:21), "Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it shall eat its fruit." Its meaning: "those who love it shall eat its fruit" — one who loves the tongue, being a man who desires to speak continually, the proper counsel for him is that he eat its fruit, that he not speak idle words, but words of Torah and wisdom and ethical instruction, and bring peace between a man and his fellow, to justify the multitude and praise the good and condemn the evil and be zealous for truth — for he can acquire for his soul endless merits through his tongue, as was stated at the outset, that life is in the tongue.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:211: Now, the faction of those who speak evil speech divides into six parts. The first part — when a man imputes a blemish to a person that is not truly in him. Sometimes, instead of beauty, he casts blame; and behold, his heart and his mouth here combine the trait of two evil factions, those being the faction of liars and the faction of those who speak evil speech. And we have been warned by the Torah not to accept evil speech, lest it be false and a lying matter, as it is said (Exodus 23:1), "You shall not accept a false report." And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 17:4), "An evildoer gives heed to wicked lips; a liar listens to a mischievous tongue." Its meaning: two factions accept evil speech. The one is the man of evil and presumption, in the sense of (Isaiah 9:16), "for everyone is a flatterer and an evildoer" — for he suspects the innocent, and loves to find fault and blame in his fellow and shame upon his honor; and when he hears his friend telling him evil speech, the presumption of his own heart leads him to believe the words are true. And the second faction — the man of falsehood, who also gives ear to and believes a mischievous tongue, for since he does not distance himself from falsehood, he does not worry whether his soul accepts a lie or whether he takes up a false report; therefore he hastens to accept evil speech — "mischievous" being like "a man of falsehood," and so (Jeremiah 9:4[5]), "your dwelling is in the midst of deceit" meaning "in the midst of men of deceit," (Psalms 109:4), "but I am prayer" meaning "a man of prayer."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:212: And know that when the listener acknowledges the evil speech, his lot and portion is one and the same as that of the one who tells the evil speech; for people will say, Behold, the listeners have accepted the matter, and this is a sign that it is true and correct — even if the listener merely inclined his ear and made himself appear to listen attentively and believe the matters, before other people. This too helps toward evil, brings shame upon his fellow, and strengthens the hands of one who brings a bad report about people. And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 25:23), "The north wind brings forth rain, and an indignant face a backbiting tongue." Its meaning: just as the north wind scatters the clouds and withholds the rain, so does an indignant face restrain evil speech — for when the teller sees the face of the listener to be indignant, the roaring sound of his words' rain will cease; but if he sees that the listener will hear him out, he will drink up iniquity like water, and will not withhold his mouth from his lies, and it will be the same tomorrow, for he will repeat his folly, continually telling falsehood. And his tongue will return after the rain of his lies — "techolel" being in the sense of "cease" (chalilah), and likewise (Numbers 30:3), "he shall not break (yachel) his word" meaning he shall not nullify it, and likewise (Genesis 4:26), "then it was begun (huchal) to call" meaning it was withheld [i.e., an alternate reading].
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:213: Solomon the king, peace upon him, further said (Proverbs 26:28), "A lying tongue hates its dachav" (translated here: those it has crushed/the humble). Its meaning: the humble, crushed, and lowly-spirited man hates a lying tongue; he will not consent to it or listen to it, for the humble man desires the honor of creatures and is grieved at their shame and disgrace. (The letter vav in "dachav" stands in place of the root's heh, as in the vav of "anav," "humble.") And some explain: the master of a lying tongue hates those who crush him and those who rebuke him, and will not further bring to them a bad report of people. And behold, we have been warned by what is written (Exodus 23:1), "You shall not accept a false report" — that we should not believe in our heart a report of evil speech so as to hold in our thought that the matters are true, thereby demeaning in our own eyes the one about whom they were said.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:214: The second part — one who speaks evil speech yet keeps distant from falsehood in it; and it is to this that they referred in saying "the faction of those who speak evil speech," even though they are not of the faction of liars. Now, if a man mentions to his fellow, between the two of them alone, the evil deeds of his fellow's ancestors, he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 25:17), "You shall not wrong one another" — Scripture speaking here of wronging through words, as we have already stated. And it is said (Ezekiel 18:20), "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father." And if he shames him over his ancestors' deeds in front of others, of this our Sages said that one who shames his fellow publicly is among those who descend to Gehinnom and do not ascend. And if he relates and makes known the abominations of his fellow's ancestors before other people, not in his presence, to make his reputation stink and demean him in the eyes of the people of his own nation, of this they said that the faction that speaks evil speech does not receive the presence of the Divine Presence. And likewise, if the fellow was a penitent, and one speaks of his former iniquities.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:215: And know that if a man sees that his fellow transgressed a matter of Torah in secret, and he reveals his sin at the gate of the multitude, he shall surely bear guilt for this — for perhaps that sinner has already turned back from his evil way, and his own thoughts already grieve him, and his own heart knows the bitterness of his soul; and it is not proper to reveal these except to a discreet sage who will not relate it to the rest of the multitude, but will merely keep his distance from the sinner's company until it becomes known to him that he has turned back from his evil way. And if the sinner is a Torah scholar and a man who fears sin, it is fitting to assume of him that he has truly done teshuvah; and even if his inclination overpowered him once, his soul will be bitter to him afterward.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:216: And one who speaks evil speech has two things calling out against him: the harm and the shame he brings about for his fellow, and his choice to condemn and declare his fellows guilty and his joy at their misfortune. And in one respect, the iniquity of one who speaks evil speech about a true matter is greater than one who speaks about a false matter — for the people will believe, when he tells true things about his fellow, and his stench will rise before them, and he will become an object of contempt in their eyes, even after he has repented of his evil and been forgiven for his sin.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:217: And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 14:9-10), "Fools mock at guilt, but among the upright there is good will. The heart knows its own bitterness, and a stranger does not share in its joy." Its meaning: the fool mocks with guilt, for he searches out people's flaws and their guilt and casts blame upon them, and never speaks of the praise and good found in them. And the parable for this: flies always come and settle upon places of filth. And it says "fools mock," using a singular verb form for each and every one of the fools, as in (Genesis 49:22), "daughters walk upon the wall." And our Sages said: whoever is disqualified himself disqualifies others and does not speak in praise of the world; his way is to disqualify people by his own flaw. "But among the upright there is good will," for it is the way of the upright to cover over all transgressions and to praise a man when some good is found in him. And they mentioned in the ethical teachings that a certain man and a certain sage passed by a carcass; the man said, How putrid is this carcass! The sage said, How white are its teeth! And it says afterward, "The heart knows its own bitterness" — and every wise man knows that Solomon would not have included among his choice ethical teachings words of no use; rather, the matter comes to explain the first verse, to declare the evil of the fool who mocks with guilt — for it is possible that the sinner has turned back from his way, and his soul is bitter to him, yet no one knows the bitterness of a man's soul, nor his joy, but himself; and he bears his guilt, since the essence of teshuvah lies in the bitterness of the heart. Therefore the fool who mentions his iniquity sins and incurs guilt.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:218: And you must know that the punishment of the fool who mocks with guilt applies only when he casts blame upon a God-fearing man whose inclination overpowered him and who transgressed and became guilty — for his custom and his way is to regret his sins, all the more so if it has become known that he has done teshuvah. But a man whose way you know and have examined, that there is no dread of God before his eyes, and who continually stands firm on an evil path — it is a mitzvah to speak of his disgrace and reveal his sins, to make transgressors stink in people's eyes, so that the souls of those who hear may be revolted by the evil deeds. And it is said (Proverbs 29:27), "An abomination to the righteous is a man of iniquity," and it is said (Proverbs 8:13), "The fear of the Lord is to hate evil." And they said: a wicked man who is the son of a righteous man, one is permitted to call him "wicked, son of a wicked man"; a righteous man who is the son of a wicked man, one is permitted to call him "righteous, son of a righteous man." And behold, when you see a man who speaks something or does some deed, and there is room to judge his word and his deed both toward guilt and toward merit — if that man is God-fearing, you are obligated to judge him favorably in a manner consistent with truth, even if the matter is closer and leans more, by strict reasoning, toward guilt. And if he is among the intermediate people, who are careful about sin yet sometimes stumble in it, you must incline the doubt and decide it in favor of merit, as our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever judges his fellow favorably, the Omnipresent judges him favorably — and this is a positive commandment of the Torah, as it is said (Leviticus 19:15), "in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor." And if the matter leans toward guilt, it should remain for you as a matter of doubt, and do not decide it toward guilt. But if that man's deeds are mostly evil, or you have examined him and found there is no fear of God in his heart, you should decide his deeds and words toward guilt, as it is said, "The wise man deals intelligently, but the house of the wicked he perverts to evil" — and we have already explained its meaning for you earlier.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:219: And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 24:28-29), "Be not a witness against your fellow without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work." Its meaning: he did not need to warn, Do not be a false witness — but he said, Do not be a witness without cause; for if your fellow has become ensnared in a sin, do not testify against him, and do not reveal his sin without cause, without rebuke. For is it really so that if a man robbed or oppressed his fellow, he must testify concerning this so that the stolen goods be restored, on the word of two witnesses — and if there is only one witness there, an oath shall pass between the two of them? But if he saw that his fellow stumbled in a matter of immorality, or in one of the other transgressions, it is not fitting that he testify concerning this without cause — meaning, without rebuke — even though he has a second witness to establish the matter. And if the sinner is a God-fearing man, it is fitting for him to speak to his own heart, for surely he has done teshuvah; also, it is fitting for him to fear for his own soul and say in his heart, After all, the man is God-fearing, and perhaps his merits outweigh his iniquities — and our Sages said that a man whose merits outweigh his iniquities is among the company of the righteous. Indeed, if the sinner is among the fools whose custom is to repeat their folly, it is good that they tell the judges, to discipline him and separate him from the prohibition. But if there is only one witness, it is not good for a man to testify alone against his fellow, for his testimony is for nothing, since it is not relied upon, as it is said (Deuteronomy 19:15), "One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity or for any sin." Therefore he shall be reckoned as one who brings forth an evil name. And the word "vahafitita" ["and deceive"] is, by transposition, like "hasibota" ["you have caused"] — meaning that with your lips you grind his face (in the sense of crumbling it into crumbs) through the great shame you cause when you reveal his hidden iniquity. And it says afterward, Do not say, As he has done to me, so I will do to him — for even if he has revealed your sin, you shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge to do to him as he did to you. And this is an honored ethical teaching, among the foundations of the fear of God. But if the sinner is a man who does not fear God — like one who casts off the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven from himself, and is not careful about a single transgression that the whole gate of his people knows to be a transgression — it is permitted to shame him and speak of his disgrace. So our Sages said, concerning (Leviticus 25:17), "You shall not wrong one another": a people who are with you in Torah and mitzvot, do not wrong through words; but one who has not set his heart to the word of the Lord, it is permitted to shame him for his deeds and to make known his abominations and pour contempt upon him. They further said: flatterers are publicized, because of the desecration of the Name. But if he stumbled in sin by way of chance, and it is his way most of the time to guard himself from iniquity, one should not reveal his sin, as we have explained. And it is also possible to explain "Be not a witness against your fellow without cause" as referring to testifying against him concerning transgressions in which you yourself, too, have been sickened just as he has — for on this account he is called "your fellow"; and this is shown by its saying afterward, Do not say, As he has done to me, so I will do to him. For even though it is a mitzvah to publicize sinners themselves and flatterers, if a fellow shares the same wickedness or the same sins as another, he should not publicize him — for his intent in revealing his hidden matters is not for good, but to rejoice at his misfortune. And second, how is it that he is not ashamed to mention against another the blemish of those very deeds which he himself holds onto? And it is said (Hosea 1:4), "and I will visit the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" — behold, even though he performed a mitzvah in cutting off the house of Ahab, he bore his own iniquity, for he too was full of transgression.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:220: And our Sages said that one who testifies alone against his fellow concerning a matter of transgression is given lashes of rebellion; but he may reveal the matter discreetly to his teacher or to a man of his confidence, if he knows that his words will be believed like the words of two witnesses. And if he has a second witness with him, the judges may hear their words to discipline the sinner discreetly, without shaming him publicly, as it is said (Leviticus 19:17), "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:221: And know that in matters between a man and his fellow, such as robbery, oppression, damage, distress, shame, and wronging through words, one may relate these matters to other people; even a lone witness who sees may tell it, in order to help the one who was wronged and to be zealous for the truth. And behold, the Torah says that a single witness may testify in court concerning a monetary claim, to obligate the defendant to take an oath — yet even so, he must first rebuke the man.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:222: The third part — the talebearer. We have been warned against this by the Torah, as it is said (Leviticus 19:16), "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" — and this too is called evil speech, and is included in the faction of those who speak evil speech, as our Sages of blessed memory mentioned concerning Doeg the Edomite, who was a master of evil speech, for he told Saul, saying to him, David came to the house of Ahimelech. And the harm of talebearing is beyond counting, for it multiplies hatred in the world and causes people to stumble in transgressing what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 19:17), "You shall not hate your brother in your heart." And behold, the world stands upon peace, and because of hatred the earth and all its inhabitants melt away, as we have already explained. And many times the talebearer places a sword in his fellow's hand to kill his own friend, as it is written (Ezekiel 22:9), "Men of talebearing were in you, to shed blood." And it is said (Jeremiah 6:28), "They are all grievous rebels, walking as talebearers; they are bronze and iron, they are all corrupters." And our Sages called talebearing "the third tongue," because it kills three: the one who says it, the one who accepts it, and the one about whom it is said — as you know from the matter of Doeg, who was driven by talebearing, and the priests were killed, and Saul was punished for accepting the tale.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:223: And our Sages of blessed memory said concerning the matter of talebearing: even though it is forbidden to accept it and to hate one's fellow because of it, one should not scorn the matter, but guard his soul and be wary of the matters. And they said, of blessed memory: in the generation of Saul there were informers among them, such as Doeg and the Ziphites, and because of this they would go down to battle and fall. In the generation of Ahab there were no informers among them, as you know from the matter of the prophets who hid themselves from Jezebel, as it is written (I Kings 18:22), "I, even I only, remain a prophet of the Lord" — and Obadiah hid a hundred prophets from them, and no man revealed that there was a prophet in Israel other than Elijah; and because of this they would go down to battle and be victorious, even though Ahab worshipped idols.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:224: And one who stirs up strife between brothers and friends, and brings hatred between them, is worse than all the parts of evil speech, as it is said (Proverbs 6:19), "and one who sends forth strife among brothers." And our Sages said that this seventh [category, or matter] is worse than all of them, as we have already stated for you in the Gates of the Fear of Sin.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:225: And a man is obligated to keep secret a confidence which his fellow reveals to him privately, even though the revealing of that secret would not itself be a matter of talebearing — for revealing the secret causes harm to its owner and is a cause of disrupting his plans, as it is said (Proverbs 15:22), "Plans are frustrated for want of counsel [secrecy]." And the second reason: one who reveals a secret has departed from the way of modesty, and thereby disregards the wishes of the secret's owner. And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 20:19), "He who reveals a secret is a talebearer." Its meaning: if you see a man who is not master over his own spirit enough to guard his tongue from revealing a secret — even though there is no matter of talebearing between one man and another in the exposure of that secret — this trait will bring him to become a talebearer, which is among the four evil factions, since his lips are not in his own power to guard. He further said (Proverbs 11:13), "A talebearer reveals secrets." Its meaning: do not entrust a secret to one who goes about as a talebearer, for since he does not guard his lips from talebearing, do not trust him with the concealment of your secret, even though you have handed your words into his keeping in a manner of secrecy and confidence. And we have been warned by the Torah not to accept evil speech, as it is said (Exodus 23:1), "You shall not accept a false report," and it is said (Proverbs 29:12), "If a ruler gives heed to lies, all his servants become wicked." Our Sages of blessed memory explained that when the ruler accepts evil speech and words of talebearing, his servants become wicked and talebearers themselves, in order to find favor in their master's eyes. And behold, our Sages, of blessed memory, intended these three parts we have mentioned when they spoke of "the faction of those who speak evil speech."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:226: The fourth part — the dust of evil speech. Our Sages said: most of the world stumbles in robbery, a minority in sexual immorality, but all in the dust of evil speech. And they said that the matter of the dust of evil speech is when a man, through his own words, brings it about that other people relate evil speech. And they said: a man should never speak of his fellow's good qualities, for out of speaking of his good, one may come to speak of his disgrace. Now, we must explain this teaching, for it is a known matter that it is among the fitting traits to speak in praise of the wise and the righteous, as it is said (Proverbs 25:27), "and to search into their own glory is glory." And they spoke of the fool who does not speak in praise of the world — but this is the character of this matter: that one should not speak of a man's good qualities except privately, one to one — meaning, when a man speaks to his fellow, not in a public assembly or a gathering of many, until it becomes known to him that there is no one present in that gathering who hates and envies the man he speaks well of. And if he wishes to praise a man who is already firmly established among the people of his nation and known to be a worthy man, in whom no evil or guilt is found, he may praise him even in the presence of a hater and an envier, for the hater cannot find fault with him; and if he does condemn him, everyone will know that his mouth spoke falsehood, and his own tongue will become a snare to his own soul.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:227: Our Sages, of blessed memory, further mentioned concerning the matter of evil speech and said: behold, if a woman asked her neighbor to bring her fire from the hearth, and she answered and said, Where indeed are there burning coals except in such-and-such a house, where they always roast meat and eat — this and the like is the dust of evil speech. And it is said (Proverbs 27:14), "He who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him." And our Sages explained this verse concerning one who praises his fellow with a praise that leads to loss — such as the matter of a guest who went out into the city square and cried out with a loud voice, relating what good the host had done him, that he slaughtered an animal and prepared it for the guest who came to him. And it happened that when the guest's account was heard, worthless men gathered and turned aside to the house of the host [to take advantage]. And a man is obligated to guard his mouth and his tongue so that he not be suspected in his words, and that people not consider him a teller of evil speech; and if he brings himself to be suspected in this, behold, he has corrupted his own discipline, and this man shall be counted as [having spread] the dust of evil speech.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:228: Now search your innermost being to grasp the essential point of this matter. We have already stated that it is permitted to speak of the disgrace of a sinner regarding violence in his hands, if it is known that he has not abandoned his way — such as the robber and the violent man, or one who causes harm and distresses others, or one who shames another's face and makes his name stink and disgraces him, or one who speaks evil speech and has not restored what was stolen, nor paid for his damage, nor sought his fellow's forgiveness to remove his iniquity. But indeed, those who consider their way properly should first speak with the sinner, for perhaps their rebuke will succeed in turning him back from his evil way; and only if he utterly refuses should they then make known to the multitude his ways and his deeds. Now, if a man seizes upon his fellow's deed concerning some matter in which he acted maliciously against his friend, and relates his deed to people and reveals the sinner's guilt and condemns his deed with many arguments — behold, the one who relates this will be suspected in this, and people will regard him as a teller of evil speech, and will say, Even if the matter were true, it would have been fitting to first open the sinner's ear to instruction; and because he did not first rebuke him, his listener will suspect him, saying that he would not have said all these things in his fellow's presence, and that he is merely flattering him [to his face while slandering him behind his back] — in the sense of what is said (Hosea 4:4), "Yet let no man strive, nor let any man reprove" [meaning, publicly denounce without private rebuke first]. And he takes pleasure in speaking of the guilt of people whose faults make him glad and whose shame brings him honor, when not in their presence — this resembles the master of evil speech, and clings to it, being of its dust. And further, people will say the matters are not accurate and that he fabricates them from his own mind; and if not so, why did he not reveal his iniquity to his face first, and concealed it from him? Therefore our Sages said: any matter that is said in the presence of its owner does not have the character of evil speech. Its meaning: if he has first given his fellow open rebuke concerning his deed, and the other did not heed his words, he may afterward make known to people the man's guilt and evil discipline, and should not be suspected of wishing to cast blame upon his fellow. And likewise, if the one relating it is known publicly not to show favoritism to any man and not to give anyone a nickname, and speaks to a man's face whatever he says not in his presence, and fears no man — and he is also firmly established among his people as one who speaks only truth — he should not be suspected when he speaks of a man's guilt to his fellow, not in his presence. And so they mentioned in their words, of blessed memory, concerning this matter, and said: Rabbi Yosei said, In all my days I never said a thing and retracted it — meaning, I never said a thing about a man not in his presence and suppressed it when in his presence. They further said: any matter said in the presence of three does not have the character of evil speech. Its meaning: since many were with him at the time he related the matters, the matter surely became known to his fellow, and this is as though he said the words in his presence.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:229: The fifth part — vulgarity of the mouth. Our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever speaks vulgarly, even if a sentence of seventy good years was decreed for him, it is turned for him into evil. And Isaiah said (Isaiah 9:16), "Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, nor have mercy on their orphans and widows, for everyone is a flatterer and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks vileness; for all this His anger is not turned away, but His hand is stretched out still." And because of this, one who speaks vulgarly bears heavy iniquity and is abominable and putrid, for he has abandoned and left behind shame and modesty, the traits known to the holy seed, and walked the paths of brazenness, which is the trait of evil vulgar people. And the second reason: he has profaned the holiness of Israel, as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:6), "and they shall say, Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people" — and this man has conducted himself in the manner of loathsome fools who distance themselves from the way of reason, which is entirely fair and pleasant. His stench has risen and his foulness has ascended, and every wise and understanding man utterly detests and abhors such things. And behold, he desecrates the vessel of the intellect, which is more precious than any precious vessel, as it is said (Proverbs 20:15), "and lips of knowledge are a precious vessel." And the punishment for one who listens to vulgar speech is great, for he does not stop up his ear or separate himself from those who speak vileness; and of him it is said (Proverbs 22:14), "The mouth of strange women is a deep pit; he who is cursed of the Lord shall fall therein."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:230: And our Sages said (Pesachim 3a): a man should never let a disgraceful word come from his mouth, for behold, Scripture used eight extra letters and did not let a disgraceful word come from its mouth, as it is said (Genesis 7:8), "and of the animals that are not clean" — for at that time the unclean animal was permitted for eating, but was not fit for sacrifice; therefore "unclean" language is considered disgraceful when applied to things that are food for man. And behold, a man is obligated to be careful not to let a disgraceful word come from his mouth, even if avoiding a disgraceful expression would lead him to lengthen his words and expand his statements. And this is like a fence to guard against vulgarity of the mouth, which is among the grave transgressions, and also a fence to guard against the telling of evil speech and casting blame upon people — as our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Batra 123a), concerning the distancing of speech from disgrace, that Scripture did not speak disgracefully even concerning an unclean animal. And our Sages said (Pesachim 3b) that one of the priests said before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, My portion of the showbread came to the size of a lizard's tail — and they examined him and found in him a taint of disqualification [from the priesthood, based on the vulgar comparison he used]. Our Sages further said that a man is obligated to choose refined language in his words and to set aside language that is not refined, even if it is not disgraceful, whether in words of Torah or in conversation about worldly matters — provided that he does not lengthen his words for this reason when speaking words of Torah, for a man is obligated to teach his disciples in a concise manner. And the matter of refined language is the manner of speech and conversation that people of clear mind and eloquent speakers follow, for they weigh and recognize which expression is refined and which its alternative, as it is said (Job 15:5), "and you choose the language of the crafty," and it is said (Job 33:3), "and my lips utter knowledge clearly," and it is said (Proverbs 10:20), "Choice silver is the tongue of the righteous."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:231: The sixth part — a complainer (nirgan). Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 18:8), "The words of a complainer are like wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly." Its meaning: the complainer is a man whose way and custom is to lament and complain, continually finding fault with his fellow's deeds and words, even though his fellow deals with him in innocence and does him no wrong at all; he judges everything toward guilt and never toward merit, and turns every inadvertent error into deliberate malice. And behold, he presents himself as though oppressed and struck down, as though he bears the weight of his fellow's sin upon himself — yet he is the one who strikes and wounds, for his words go down into the innermost parts of the belly. For one who lodges complaints against his fellow when the fellow has not touched him and has done him only good — this is a storm raging in the heart, and it is like one who shoots fiery sparks that descend into the innermost parts of the belly. The word "kemitlahamim" is, by transposition, like "mitalmim" ["being struck"], in the manner of "simlah/salmah," in the sense of (Proverbs 23:35), "they struck me, but I did not feel it." It is as though it said, "the words of a complainer are like a blow." And its being said in the plural, "mitlahamim," is because "nirgan" refers collectively to all complainers, as in (Jeremiah 11:15), "and holy flesh shall pass from you" [plural verb for collective], (Isaiah 45:8), "and let salvation sprout." Solomon the king, peace upon him, further said (Proverbs 16:28), "and a complainer separates close friends." Its meaning: he separates from himself lover and friend, for they cannot bear his company. And our Sages said: do not multiply complaint, lest you come to sin. And many times the complainer, even when shown kindness, will regard it as evil, and repay evil for good — and it is said (Proverbs 17:13), "Whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house." And sometimes he thinks of the kindnesses of the Lord as though they were for vengeance and requital, in the sense of what is said (Deuteronomy 1:27), "and you complained in your tents, and said, Because the Lord hates us, He has brought us out, etc." Therefore distance yourself from the way of complainers, for their paths are crooked to them; whoever walks in it knows no peace. Train your tongue to judge favorably, and let righteousness be the girdle of your loins.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:1:
Gate Four – On the Distinctions of Atonement
Just as the body has sickness and disease, so does the soul; and the disease and sickness of the soul are its evil traits and its sins. And when the wicked man turns back from his evil way, the Blessed Name heals the sickness of the sinning soul, as it is said (Psalms 41:5), "Lord, be gracious to me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against You," and it is said (Isaiah 6:10), "and turn back and be healed." And in the manner that it sometimes happens in bodily illnesses that the illness has been lightened and most of the disease's recovery has begun, yet the body is not yet fully cleared of it except through drinking a bitter potion, and further enduring the pain of afflicting the soul from every food of desire — so is there a soul sick from great iniquity: even though most of the sickness is healed and most parts of the punishment removed after teshuvah, and the Blessed Name has turned back from His burning wrath, the soul is not yet cleared of the sickness, and its iniquity is not yet accepted, until the sinner is chastened with sufferings and corrected with pain, and evils and troubles befall him — in the sense of what is said (Genesis 4:13-14), "My iniquity is too great to bear. Behold, You have driven me out this day from the face of the earth, and from Your face shall I be hidden; and I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and it shall come to pass, that whoever finds me shall kill me." And through teshuvah, most of his iniquity was forgiven, and the essential punishment was removed, and he was saved from death, as it is said (Genesis 4:15), "And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, lest any who found him should kill him." But the punishment of exile remained upon him, as it is said, "and he dwelt in the land of Nod, east of Eden." And our Sages, of blessed memory, said that the punishment of wandering, too, was lightened for him after his teshuvah, for before this the decree of wandering had been doubled upon him, as it is said, "and I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth" — behold, it mentions the wandering in a doubled expression; but after the teshuvah it is said (Genesis 4:16), "and he dwelt in the land of Nod."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:2: And this matter is further clarified from what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 4:27-28), "And if any one of the common people sin through ignorance, while he does something against any of the commandments of the Lord concerning things which ought not to be done, and is guilty; or if his sin, which he has sinned, comes to his knowledge, etc." And our Sages of blessed memory said that a sin-offering is brought for an inadvertent transgression only in a matter for which the deliberate transgression is punished with excision. And because the iniquity of excision is so great, the atonement of the sinner is not complete even for the inadvertent version of it until he brings a sin-offering, even though he has confessed his sin — for without confession and teshuvah, his iniquity is not atoned through the sin-offering sacrifice, as it is said (Proverbs 21:27), "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination." And after confession and the offering, his iniquity is atoned, as it is said (Leviticus 4:31), "and the priest shall make atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him." And consider from this: if one who transgressed inadvertently is not clean even after teshuvah until he brings an offering, how much more severe is the punishment for the deliberate transgressor! Indeed, his iniquity is atoned through sufferings, as it is said (Job 33:19,26), "He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, etc.... he shall pray to God, and He will be favorable to him." And it is said (Proverbs 3:12), "For whom the Lord loves He rebukes, even as a father the son in whom he delights." And there is counsel and remedy for the sinner through good deeds, to shield him from the pains, as will be explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:3: This matter is further clarified in the Torah, as it is said (Leviticus 16:30), "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you, etc." Behold, the atonement of Yom Kippur is needed after teshuvah, for the essential atonement of Yom Kippur is together with teshuvah.
